--- title: "Solid Waste and Network Models" subtitle: "Lecture 18" author: "Vivek Srikrishnan" course: "BEE 4750" institution: "Cornell University" date: "November 09, 2026" format: revealjs: slide-number: c/t show-slide-number: all center-title-slide: true width: 1280 height: 720 transition: none toc: true toc-depth: 1 toc-title: "Overview" history: false link-external-newwindow: true theme: ../sass/slides.scss template-partials: - title-slide.html menu: numbers: true html-math-method: mathjax include-in-header: mathjax-config.html date-format: long email-obfuscation: javascript chalkboard: theme: whiteboard buttons: true controls: true engine: julia julia: exeflags: ["+1.11.5"] execute: freeze: auto daemon: 600 --- # Review of Last Class ## Binaries Switch Facilities On and Off An optional facility needs a **binary** $u \in \{0, 1\}$: - fixed cost $\times\, u$ in the objective (paid only if it operates); - output $\leq$ capacity $\times\, u$ (a closed facility does nothing); - output $\geq$ minimum $\times\, u$ (at least the minimum when on). **Raises the question**: what if the decisions are **flows** through a network? ::: {.notes} A binary variable turns an on/off decision into linear constraints. ::: ## Questions? :::: {.columns .center} ::: {.column width="40%"} ![](figures/vsrikrish-poll.png){fig-alt="Poll Everywhere QR Code" fig-align="center" width="100%"} ::: ::: {.column width=60%} **Text**: VSRIKRISH to 22333 **URL**: [https://pollev.com/vsrikrish](https://pollev.com/vsrikrish)

[See Results](https://www.polleverywhere.com/multiple_choice_polls/qKeig0hHShZYHAOmvZtZm?preview=true&controls=none){preview-link="true"} ::: :::: # Solid Waste Management ## Waste Load Allocation :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width=50%} Some relevant questions: - Where do we send waste? - What types of facilities do we build/operate? ::: ::: {.column width=50%} ![Waste Management Hierarchy](https://www.epa.gov/sites/default/files/styles/medium/public/2015-08/hierarchy_hierarchy_and_options_pages.png){width=100%} ::: {.caption} Source: [EPA](https://www.epa.gov/homeland-security-waste/waste-management-options-homeland-security-incidents) ::: ::: :::: ::: {.notes} A city produces waste every day and has to put it somewhere. The options form a hierarchy: reduce first, then recycle, then recover energy, and landfill last. The problem combines two kinds of decision: where each truckload goes (a routing decision that can vary continuously), and which facilities to build or keep open (an on/off decision). That combination is why this is a mixed integer problem. ::: ## Waste Allocation As A Network Want to model *flows* between waste sources and sinks (disposal sites). ![Network Representation](figures/waste-network-blank.svg){width=75%} ::: {.notes} A network has nodes (cities, facilities) and arcs (the roads between them). The decisions are how much flows along each arc. Some arcs go from one facility to another: what a facility does not fully dispose of has to be shipped on. ::: ## Network Parameterization :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width=50%} ![Network Parameterization](figures/waste-network-params.svg) ::: ::: {.column width=50%} | Variable | Definition | | :--: | :------- | | $\color{purple}S_i$ | Waste produced at source $i$ (Mg/day) | | $\color{red}K_j$ | Capacity of disposal $j$ (Mg/day) | | $\color{blue}W_{ij}$ | Waste transported from source $i$ to disposal $j$ (Mg/day) | ::: :::: ::: {.notes} Three symbols to carry through the lecture: S for what each source produces, K for what each facility can take, and W for the flow on each arc. W is the decision. Mg is a megagram, a metric ton. ::: ## Conservation at Each Node **Mass balance** at each node: a source ships everything it produces, $\sum_j W_{ij} = S_i$. A facility passes on a fixed fraction of what arrives. A transfer station receives 40 Mg/day from each of two cities and sends it all to a landfill ($T_L$) or a recycler ($T_R$). **What is its mass-balance constraint?** ::: {.fragment .fade-in} $$T_L + T_R = 40 + 40 = 80 \text{ Mg/day}$$ ::: ::: {.notes} Conservation holds at every node: nothing is created or destroyed at a node, only routed or transformed. At the transfer station, what leaves equals what arrives. A facility is the same idea with a transformation: a recycler that recovers 40% passes on the other 60%. ::: ## What Is Missing? The network captures the graph structure of the system, but nothing else. **What else might we need?** ::: {.fragment .fade-in} - System dynamics (fate & transport) - Objectives - Costs - Management goals and/or regulatory constraints ::: ::: {.notes} The graph says what is connected to what; it says nothing about what an MRF or a WTE does to the waste, what anything costs, or what the rules are. All of that has to come from outside the network. ::: # Waste Management Example ## Example System :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width=60%} ![Waste Management Example](figures/waste-example-network.svg) ::: ::: {.column width=40%} Three disposal options: - Waste-to-Energy (WTE) - Materials Recovery Facility (MRF) - Landfill (LF) ::: :::: ::: {.notes} Two cities, producing 100 and 170 Mg/day, and three facilities with the capacities in red. Distances in blue. Note the arcs between facilities: the MRF sends its residual to the WTE or the landfill, and the WTE sends its ash to the landfill. ::: ## Decision Variables ***What are our decision variables?*** ::: {.fragment .fade-in} Variable | Definition :--: | :----- $W_{ij}$ | Waste transported from city $i$ to disposal $j$ (Mg/day) $R_{kj}$ | Residual waste transported from disposal $k$ to disposal $j$ (Mg/day) $Y_j$ | Operational status (on/off) of disposal $j$ (binary) ::: ::: {.notes} Three kinds: flows from cities (W), flows of residuals between facilities (R), and whether each facility operates (Y, binary). The residual flows here are R21 (MRF to WTE), R23 (MRF to landfill), and R13 (WTE ash to landfill). The facility numbering is WTE 1, MRF 2, landfill 3. ::: ## What Does It Cost? - **Transportation**: a cost $a_{ij}$ (\$/Mg-km) times the distance $l_{ij}$ (km) from $i$ to $j$ times the flow, $\sum_{i, j} a_{ij} \, l_{ij} \, W_{ij}$, plus residuals. - **Disposal**: a fixed cost $c_j$ (\$/day) and a tipping cost $b_j$ (\$/Mg). ::: {.fragment .fade-in} $$\text{Disposal cost} = \sum_j \left[c_j + b_j \times (\text{everything arriving at } j)\right]$$ **Is this right?** ::: ::: {.notes} Board item: the two cost components. The problem is the fixed cost: as written, every facility pays it even if it receives nothing. ::: ## Fixed Costs Need an On/Off Variable The fixed cost is paid **only if the facility operates**: $$Y_j = \begin{cases}0 & \text{if facility } j \text{ is not operated} \\ 1 & \text{if facility } j \text{ is operated} \end{cases}$$ ::: {.fragment .fade-in} $$\text{Disposal cost} = \sum_j \left[c_j \, Y_j + b_j \times (\text{everything arriving at } j)\right]$$ ::: ::: {.notes} This is the fixed-cost pattern: fixed cost times the binary. On its own it is not enough, because nothing yet stops waste from being sent to a facility with Y equal to zero. The capacity constraint will close that gap. ::: ## The Example's Costs | Facility | Fixed cost (\$/yr) | Fixed cost (\$/day) | Tipping (\$/Mg) | Capacity (Mg/day) | |:--|--:|--:|--:|--:| | WTE | 900,000 | 2,466 | 60 | 150 | | MRF | 400,000 | 1,096 | 5 | 130 | | LF | 700,000 | 1,918 | 40 | 200 | Transport costs \$1\.50/Mg-km. The MRF recycles 40% of what it receives, at \$35/Mg recycled, and passes on the rest; the WTE leaves 20% of its input as ash. ::: {.notes} The daily fixed costs are the annual costs divided by 365. The MRF is cheap to run but does not dispose of the rest: the 60% it does not recycle still has to go to the WTE or the landfill. ::: ## Working Out One Cost Coefficient :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width=48%} Sending 1 Mg from City 1 to the MRF (5 km) costs $$\underbrace{1.5 \times 5}_{\text{haul}} + \underbrace{5}_{\text{tip}} + \underbrace{0.4 \times 35}_{\text{recycle}}$$ = **\$26.5/Mg**. ::: ::: {.column width=52%} | \$/Mg | WTE | MRF | LF | |:--|--:|--:|--:| | City 1 | 82.5 | 26.5 | 85 | | City 2 | 75 | 41.5 | 77.5 | | MRF residual | 82.5 | — | 88 | | WTE ash | — | — | 67 | ::: :::: ::: {.notes} The worked coefficient: haul 5 km at \$1\.50 a Mg-km, tip \$5, and recycle 40% of each Mg at \$35 per Mg recycled. Every other entry is built the same way; for example, City 1 to the WTE is 1\.5 × 15 + 60 = 82\.5. The residual rows include the tipping cost at the facility receiving them. ::: ## Mass Balance for Cities and Residuals :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width=45%} **Cities** ship everything they produce: $W_{11} + W_{12} + W_{13} =$ 100 $W_{21} + W_{22} + W_{23} =$ 170 ::: ::: {.column width=55%} ::: {.fragment .fade-in} **Residuals** (fate and transport): WTE ash: $$R_{13} = 0.2\,(W_{11} + W_{21} + R_{21})$$ MRF residual: $$R_{21} + R_{23} = 0.6\,(W_{12} + W_{22})$$ ::: ::: :::: ::: {.notes} These are mass-balance constraints. The city ones say every Mg goes somewhere. The residual ones describe what each facility does to the waste: the WTE leaves 20% of everything it burns as ash, including residual from the MRF, and the ash must be landfilled; the MRF passes on 60% of what it receives. Likely question: what is "residual"? What a facility passes on after processing: the MRF's unrecycled waste and the WTE's ash. ::: ## Linking Capacity to On/Off Capacity counts all waste arriving at a facility, and multiplying it by $Y_j$ means a closed facility receives nothing: $$ \begin{aligned} \text{WTE:}& \quad W_{11} + W_{21} + R_{21} \leq 150\,Y_1 \\ \text{MRF:}& \quad W_{12} + W_{22} \leq 130\,Y_2 \\ \text{LF:}& \quad W_{13} + W_{23} + R_{13} + R_{23} \leq 200\,Y_3 \end{aligned} $$ **Which constraints need a binary, and why?** ::: {.fragment .fade-in} Any that must change when a facility closes: the capacities. ::: ::: {.notes} Likely question: why is the binary in the capacity constraint? This one constraint per facility does two jobs: it is the capacity limit when the facility is open, and it forces every incoming flow to zero when it is closed. That is why Y belongs here and not in the city balances. The test for any constraint is whether it has to change when the facility is closed. The residual balances don't: once nothing arrives at a closed facility, its residual is zero anyway. A minimum feed (this model has none) would need Y too, as flow in at least the minimum times Y; otherwise it would force a closed facility to take waste. Make sure the landfill line includes the residual and ash arriving from the other facilities. ::: ## The Full Problem $$ \begin{aligned} \min_{\mathbf{W}, \mathbf{R}, \mathbf{Y}} \quad & \sum_{i, j} C_{ij} W_{ij} + \sum_{k, j} C^R_{kj} R_{kj} + \sum_j c_j Y_j \\ \text{subject to:} \quad & \textstyle\sum_j W_{ij} = S_i \\ & \text{residual out of } k = \text{fraction} \times \text{input to } k \\ & \textstyle\sum_i W_{ij} + \sum_k R_{kj} \leq K_j\,Y_j \\ & W_{ij},\, R_{kj} \geq 0, \quad Y_j \in \{0, 1\} \end{aligned} $$ $C_{ij}$, $C^R_{kj}$: cost per Mg sent from city $i$, or of residual sent from facility $k$, to facility $j$ (\$/Mg): haul, tip and, at the MRF, recycle. ::: {.notes} The same problem in general form. It is a mixed integer linear program: linear in everything, with three binary variables. ::: # Solving It ## Solving the Example in JuMP ::: {#14 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code code-fold="true"} function solve_waste(; landfill_capacity=capacity[3]) cap = [capacity[1], capacity[2], landfill_capacity] model = Model(HiGHS.Optimizer) set_silent(model) @variable(model, W[1:2, 1:3] >= 0) # city i -> facility j [Mg/day] @variable(model, R21 >= 0) # MRF residual -> WTE @variable(model, R23 >= 0) # MRF residual -> LF @variable(model, R13 >= 0) # WTE ash -> LF @variable(model, Y[1:3], Bin) # facility operates? @objective(model, Min, sum(city_cost[i, j] * W[i, j] for i in 1:2, j in 1:3) + cost_R21 * R21 + cost_R23 * R23 + cost_R13 * R13 + sum(fixed_cost[j] * Y[j] for j in 1:3)) @constraint(model, city[i in 1:2], sum(W[i, :]) == waste[i]) @constraint(model, ash, R13 == ash_rate * (W[1, 1] + W[2, 1] + R21)) @constraint(model, residual, R21 + R23 == (1 - recycle_rate) * (W[1, 2] + W[2, 2])) @constraint(model, wte, W[1, 1] + W[2, 1] + R21 <= cap[1] * Y[1]) @constraint(model, mrf, W[1, 2] + W[2, 2] <= cap[2] * Y[2]) @constraint(model, lf, W[1, 3] + W[2, 3] + R13 + R23 <= cap[3] * Y[3]) optimize!(model) return (cost=objective_value(model), W=value.(W), R21=value(R21), R23=value(R23), R13=value(R13), Y=round.(Int, value.(Y)), lf_load=value(W[1, 3] + W[2, 3] + R13 + R23), cap=cap) end base = solve_waste() ``` ::: The optimal cost is **\$26,881/day**, and all 3 facilities operate. ::: {.notes} Open the fold: each constraint from the previous slides appears once, with Y declared `Bin` and each capacity multiplied by Y. ::: ## The Solution :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width=55%} ![Waste Management Problem Solution](figures/waste-example-solution.svg) ::: ::: {.column width=45%} | Flow | Mg/day | |:--|--:| | City 1 → MRF | 100 | | City 2 → LF | 170 | | MRF residual → WTE | 37\.5 | | MRF residual → LF | 22\.5 | | WTE ash → LF | 7\.5 | ::: :::: ::: {.notes} City 1 sends everything to the nearby MRF. City 2 sends everything to the landfill. The MRF's residual is split between the WTE and the landfill, and the WTE's ash goes to the landfill too. ::: ## Why Is the WTE Open? The WTE costs \$2,466/day just to open. **Why pay that to burn 37\.5 Mg/day?** ::: {.fragment .fade-in} Because the **landfill is full**: it takes 200 of its 200 Mg/day. The MRF's residual has to go somewhere, and the only other place is the WTE. The landfill's capacity constraint is **binding**. ::: ::: {.notes} Likely question: why is the WTE open if it is expensive? Because the landfill is exactly full, and the MRF's residual has to go somewhere. ::: ## What If the Landfill Were Bigger? ``` {.julia .cell-code code-fold="true"} bigger = solve_waste(landfill_capacity=220) println("| Landfill capacity (Mg/day) | Cost (\\\$/day) | WTE | MRF | LF |") println("|:--|--:|:--:|:--:|:--:|") for r in (base, bigger) status = fill("open", 3) for j in 1:3 if r.Y[j] == 0 status[j] = "**closed**" end end println("| ", r.cap[3], " | ", commas(r.cost), " | ", join(status, " | "), " |") end ``` | Landfill capacity (Mg/day) | Cost (\$/day) | WTE | MRF | LF | |:--|--:|:--:|:--:|:--:| | 200 | 26,881 | open | open | open | | 220 | 24,539 | **closed** | open | open | With 20 Mg/day more landfill, the **WTE closes** and the system saves \$2,342/day. City 2 now sends 25 Mg/day to the MRF, and all 75 Mg/day of the MRF's residual goes to the landfill. ::: {.notes} With a 220 Mg/day landfill, the MRF's residual fits in the landfill and the WTE is no longer worth its fixed cost. ::: # Key Takeaways ## Key Takeaways - A network model's decisions are **flows** on arcs, constrained by **conservation** at each node. - An optional facility needs a **binary**: fixed cost $\times\, Y_j$ in the objective, and in every constraint that changes when it is closed (here, flow in $\leq K_j Y_j$). - A binding capacity at one facility can force another to open: the WTE runs only because the landfill is full. - A network graph becomes a model only with fate and transport, costs, and rules. ## Network Models Elsewhere - Can have more advanced network models with highly-specified routes - Transportation networks - Power transmission networks - Pipeline networks - Can also add flow constraints rather than just mass-balance. - Flows could also be bidirectional. ::: {.notes} The same structure (flows on arcs, conservation at nodes, capacities, sometimes on/off decisions) covers transportation, power transmission, and pipelines. Power flow adds physics that determines how flow splits across lines, rather than letting the planner choose freely. ::: # Upcoming Schedule ## Next Classes **Wednesday, November 11**: Lab 3, Fixed Costs and Facility Siting in JuMP (bring a laptop). **Monday, November 16**: Quiz 5, then stochastic optimization and scenario trees. ## Assessments **HW8**: assigned Wednesday, due Thursday, November 19 (network models and waste allocation). **Project update**: due Friday, November 13. **Quiz 5**: Monday, November 16 (capacity expansion, mixed integer programming, and waste and network models). ::: {.notes} HW8 asks students to set up a different, small network themselves. ::: # Appendix ## Indicator Constraints in JuMP ```julia @variable(waste, Y[1:3], Bin) @constraint(waste, commit_mrf, !Y[2] => {W[1, 2] + W[2, 2] == 0}) ``` Some solvers let you write the on/off logic directly. This says: if $Y_2 = 0$, nothing arrives at the MRF, $W_{12} + W_{22} = 0$. For the WTE, the arriving flow also includes the MRF residual: $W_{11} + W_{21} + R_{21} = 0$ when $Y_1 = 0$. The capacity-linking constraint used in the lecture does the same job and works with every solver. ::: {.notes} Reference only. Indicator constraints are a convenience some solvers support. The linking constraint, arriving flow at most capacity times Y, is the portable way to write the same logic. ::: ## Big-M Reformulation Not every solver supports indicator constraints. The general trick is a **big-M** constraint: $$M\,Y_2 \geq W_{12} + W_{22}, \qquad M\,Y_1 \geq W_{11} + W_{21} + R_{21}$$ where $M$ is larger than any feasible value of the right-hand side. Choosing $M = K_j$ (the facility's capacity) gives exactly the capacity-linking constraint from the lecture. ::: {.notes} Reference only. A smaller valid M gives a tighter LP relaxation, which helps branch and bound; the capacity is the natural choice here because no feasible flow can exceed it. :::
